govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EvidenceFakedOt: A short file titled Fake Evidence concerns evidence said to have been faked in other cases, apart from the Kennedy case that fills most of this archive. The surviving record gives the title and its subject but no author, date, or list of the cases covered. It stands as a researcher's reference note on fabricated proof, kept with the assassination files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EvidenceNewFede:
John P. MacKenzie reported for the Washington Post on a change coming to every federal courtroom in the country. The Supreme Court had approved a new set of Federal Rules of Evidence. His article explains the rules and the impact lawyers and judges expected them to have on trials in U.S. courts.

Evidence rules decide what a jury may hear, so a new national code touched every case to come. MacKenzie's report translates a technical legal reform for general readers, setting out what would change in practice. It preserves the moment the modern federal evidence system arrived.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PicturesLifeMag:
A contents scan preserves the lineup of LIFE magazine, volume 63, number 21, dated November 24, 1967. The issue led with 'Impact of the Supershot,' a report on the success of the Saturn rocket, photographed by Ralph Morse. It also carried Ray Bradbury's 'An Impatient Gulliver Above Our Roofs.' News and features of the week filled the rest.

A contents page is a magazine in miniature: the editors' ranking of what mattered that week. In late November 1967, that meant the space race on the cover and a science-fiction writer looking down at Earth. The scan preserves the issue's shape rather than its stories, a table of contents kept as evidence of what a mass magazine offered its readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TapesRelease05-: When the White House released edited tape transcripts in 1974, William Greider of the Washington Post studied how President Nixon sounded in private. His May 29, 1974 article calls that private style fuzzy, in contrast to Nixon's public image of control. The piece ran while the Watergate scandal was closing in on the presidency. It shows reporters reading the transcripts not just for crimes, but for character.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WaldieJeromeRRe: Harold Weisberg wrote to Congressman Jerome Waldie on November 10, 1973. The letter concerns Leon Jaworski, who had just become the Watergate special prosecutor. Weisberg often carried his complaints about official investigations to members of Congress. Writing to Waldie, a California Democrat known for challenging the executive branch, fit that pattern. The letter links his assassination work to the Watergate fight then under way.
govdocs-archive_org-sscistudy1_Senate_Re:
In 2014 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released its study of the CIA's detention and interrogation program. The program ran after the September 11 attacks and held prisoners at secret sites abroad.

Senate investigators read millions of agency cables and reported what the program did, what it cost, and what it produced. Their study found harsher treatment than the public had been told, and weak proof that it gained unique information. The report became a landmark of congressional oversight, and the full text here lets readers weigh the Senate's evidence directly.
